steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction to our paper on a Koopman operator-based generalization bound for neural networks that stays meaningful for full-rank weight matrices. Review existing bound types and their limits, present our bound and how it combines with existing ones, relate it to Koopman operator work, and list contributions.

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
Generalization of neural networks and existing bounds
- generalization: big topic in NN analysis; approach: bound network complexity
- intuition: many parameters -> large complexity / generalization error; classical VC-dimension theory
- but over-parameterized NNs still generalize
- norm-based bounds: no explicit dependence on parameter count; (p,q) norms of weights; exponential in depth if norms large
- compression-based bounds: how much network can be compressed; smaller with lower rank
- low rank not the only reason: high-rank weights still generalize (empirical) -> compression bounds not always tight

Our Koopman-based bound
- this paper: completely different uniform complexity bound via Koopman operators; explains generalization with high- or full-rank weights
- notation: depth L, width d_{j} of j th layer, final nonlinearity g, n samples
- W_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{j}\times d_{j-1}} injective, s_{j}>d_{j}/2 smoothness of H_{j} where Koopman operator defined
- \|\cdot\| operator norm; E_{j}, G_{j} factors from activations and range of W_{j}

Determinant factor and orthogonal weights
- determinant factor: large singular values of W_{j} -> small bound
- tight when condition number (largest / smallest singular value) small
- orthogonal W_{j}: G_{j}=1, \|W_{j}\|^{s_{j-1}}/\operatorname{det}(W_{j}^{*}W_{j})^{1/4} reduces to 1
- interpretation: W_{j} transforms signals in certain directions, easier feature extraction
- networks with orthogonal weights exist; bound justifies their generalization

Combining with existing bounds; Koopman operator background
- our bound can be combined with / complement existing bounds
- rank of weights large near input layer, small near output layer (empirical)
- our bound for lower layers + existing bounds for higher layers -> tight, layer-aware
- determinant factors come from Koopman operators: linear operator defined by composition of functions
- used for dynamical systems and time-series from them; theoretical aspects studied
- Koopman + NNs: learning dynamics of parameters -> efficient learning algorithms; NNs to find Koopman eigenfunctions; Koopman for equilibrium models
- here instead: composition structure of NNs as Koopman operators -> complexity analysis, operator-theoretic view

Contributions
- new complexity bound with norm and determinant of weights; small when condition numbers small; justifies orthogonal-weight networks; explains high-rank generalization (Section 2, paragraph after Proposition 6, Remark 7)
- combine with existing bounds -> role of each layer (Subsection 4.4)
- operator-theoretic approach; Koopman operators give determinant term (Subsection 3.4, Subsection 4.1)
- operator-theoretic approach shows new aspect of NNs

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Understanding the generalization property has been one of the biggest topics in analyzing neural networks. One main approach to study this theoretically is to bound some complexity of the networks. Intuitively, if there are many parameters, the complexity and the generalization error become large. This intuition has been studied, for example, with classical VC-dimension theory. But for neural networks, the generalization error can be small even in over-parameterized regimes. To explain this, norm-based bounds have been studied. These bounds do not depend explicitly on the number of parameters. But they are usually written with the (p,q) norms of the weight matrices, and if the norms are large, the bounds grow exponentially with the depth of the network. Another approach for over-parameterized networks is the compression-based approach. These bounds explain generalization by looking at how much the networks can be compressed, and they get smaller when the ranks of the weight matrices get smaller. But low rank is not the only reason for generalization. Prior work showed empirically that networks generalize well even when the weight matrices are high-rank. So if the weight matrices have large ranks, the existing compression-based bounds are not always tight.

In this paper we derive a completely different kind of uniform complexity bound using Koopman operators, and it sheds light on why networks generalize well even when their weights are high- or full-rank matrices. More precisely, let L be the depth, d_{j} the width of the j th layer, g the final nonlinear transformation, and n the number of samples. For j=1,\ldots,L, let W_{j}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{j}\times d_{j-1}} be an injective weight matrix, and s_{j}>d_{j}/2 describes the smoothness of a function space H_{j} where the Koopman operator is defined. Our results are summarized as follows, where \|\cdot\| is the operator norm, and E_{j} and G_{j} are factors determined by the activation functions and the range of W_{j}, respectively:

Surprisingly, the determinant factor says that the bound gets small if the singular values of W_{j} are large. The bound is tight when the condition number of W_{j}, i.e., the ratio between the largest and the smallest singular values, is small. In particular, when W_{j} is orthogonal, G_{j}=1 and the factor \|W_{j}\|^{s_{j-1}}/\operatorname{det}(W_{j}^{*}W_{j})^{1/4} reduces to 1. One way to interpret this is that W_{j} transforms signals in certain directions, and this makes it easy for the network to extract features of the data. Networks with orthogonal weight matrices have been proposed before, and our bound also justifies the generalization property of these networks.

Besides giving a new perspective, our bound can also be combined with existing bounds, so it can work as a complement to them. Earlier work pointed out that the rank of the weight matrix tends to be large near the input layer and small near the output layer. If we use our bound for the lower layers and existing bounds for the higher layers, we get a tight bound that takes the role of each layer into account. The determinant factors come from Koopman operators. A Koopman operator is a linear operator defined by the composition of functions. It has been studied for analyzing dynamical systems and time-series data generated from dynamical systems, and its theoretical aspects have been studied as well. The connection between Koopman operators and neural networks has also been discussed. For example, efficient learning algorithms have been proposed by describing the learning dynamics of the parameters of neural networks with Koopman operators. Another work used neural networks to identify eigenfunctions of Koopman operators in order to extract features of dynamical systems, and another used Koopman operators to analyze equilibrium models. In this paper, on the other hand, we represent the composition structure of neural networks with Koopman operators, and use them to analyze the complexity of neural networks from an operator-theoretic perspective.

Our main contributions are the following:

- We show a new complexity bound, which involves both the norm and the determinant of the weight matrices. Because of the determinant term, our bound gets small if the condition numbers of the weight matrices get small. In particular, it justifies the generalization property of existing networks with orthogonal weight matrices. It also gives a new perspective on why networks with high-rank weights generalize well (Section 2, the paragraph after Proposition 6, and Remark 7).

- Our bound can be combined with existing bounds to get a bound that describes the role of each layer (Subsection 4.4).

- We give an operator-theoretic approach for analyzing networks. We use Koopman operators to derive the determinant term in our bound (Subsection 3.4 and Subsection 4.1).

We want to emphasize that our operator-theoretic approach shows a new aspect of neural networks.

By adopting our bound for lower layers and existing bounds for higher layers, we obtain a tight bound that takes the role of each layer into account. The determinant factors come from Koopman operators. Koopman operator is a linear operator defined by the composition of functions. It has been investigated for analyzing dynamical systems and time-series data generated from dynamical systems [21,22,23,24,25,26,27,28]. Its theoretical aspects have also been studied [29,30,31,32]. Connections between Koopman operators and neural networks have also been discussed. For example, efficient learning algorithms are proposed by describing the learning dynamics of the parameters of neural networks by Koopman operators [33,34]. [35] applied neural networks to identifying eigenfunctions of Koopman operators to extract features of dynamical systems. [36] applied Koopman operators to analyze equilibrium models. On the other hand, in this paper, we represent the composition structure of neural networks using Koopman operators, and apply them to analyzing the complexity of neural networks from an operator-theoretic perspective.

Our main contributions are as follows:

- • We show a new complexity bound, which involves both the norm and determinant of the weight matrices. By virtue of the determinant term, our bound gets small if the condition numbers of the weight matrices get small. Especially, it justifies the generalization property of existing networks with orthogonal weight matrices. It also provides a new perspective about why the networks with high-rank weights generalize well (Section 2, the paragraph after Proposition 6, and Remark 7).

- • We can combine our bound with existing bounds to obtain a bound which describes the role of each layer (Subsection 4.4).

- • We provide an operator-theoretic approach to analyzing networks. We use Koopman operators to derive the determinant term in our bound (Subsection 3.4 and Subsection 4.1).

We emphasize that our operator-theoretic approach shows a new aspect of neural networks.
